title: When Machines Have the Answers, Build Better Humans With AI Augmentation Not Automation (Vivienne Ming, Scientist, Professor, Author)
author: Vivienne Ming

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Pragmatic adoption: Experimentation outruns transformation evidence
st.an: The excerpt consists of promotional closing remarks about supporting Ming’s philanthropy and companies. It provides no substantive claim, evidence or prediction about pragmatic AI adoption, experimentation, organisational implementation or demonstrated transformation, so its position relative to the cluster cannot be determined.
qs: But really, you're just supporting the work at my philanthropy.
But you can also find out about some of my companies working in Alzheimer's, working in AI for Science, and I think just supporting the work that we're doing would be amazing.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Ming accepts the cluster’s core augmentation and work-redesign proposition, then materially extends it with forecasting evidence that active human–AI co-creation can outperform passive reliance and with a concrete prescription for deeply integrated workflows. She also reinforces the cluster’s concerns about inadequate collaboration benchmarks, weak organisational absorption and junior-development risks.
qs: But there was a group of people that pushed back, used the AI to challenge their assumptions and challenge the AI's assumption, and they did really well.
And you should really think through a deep integrative workflow for the human machine to be working together.

kp.k: Forecasting experiment favored deeply integrated human–AI collaboration
kp.d: Ming reports recruiting around UC Berkeley and Greater Berkeley to forecast meaningful economic and international-relations events drawn from Polymarket. Forecasting was chosen because AI could not have memorized future outcomes. Unlike the host's initial characterization of a small AI advantage, Ming says the worst AI tested, a small open-source model, substantially outperformed the best unaided participant; the prediction market still outperformed AI. Participants who deeply co-created with AI approached market performance on 10 predictions in one hour. The transcript supplies no total sample size or numerical accuracy scores.
qs: The worst AI we looked at, which is a little open source model, did vastly better than the best human being.
Well, they can't memorize the future.
Although the AI didn't do as well as the prediction market itself.

So only the cyborgs where the human machine were co-creating their forecasts, did we see what it turns out not only super AI performance, they did nearly as well as polymarket, which given naive people, one hour, 10 predictions, and they were doing as well as experts betting millions of dollars.

kp.k: Passive delegation and final approval undermined collaborative performance
kp.d: Ming distinguishes copying AI answers from deep collaboration and from a sequential 'Centaur' arrangement in which AI analyzes and humans decide. Most participants copied outputs; those deciding without understanding AI's analysis or raw data performed worse than AI alone. She approximately identifies deep collaborators as 10% of Berkeley students and 5% of the general-population participants she examined, then conjectures low-single-digit prevalence in the wider population. Her claim concerns substantive engagement, not merely having a human approve the result.
qs: You put them together, the vast majority of people simply say, GPT, what will be the price of oil in six months? It gives them an answer, they copy, they paste, and they're done.
about maybe 10% to the Berkeley students, 5% to the general population that I was looking at, almost certainly low single-digit percentages, probably in the general population
One of the things we saw is people that use the AI to do the analysis and then made the decision, sometimes called the Centaur model or the human in the loop.
They did worse than the AI alone, not better.

kp.k: Complementary expertise supports augmentation rather than blanket automation
kp.d: Ming supports automating activities such as filling forms and moving data, but rejects assuming that successive automation stages followed by human approval produce the best outcomes. She cites Anthropic research, an analysis of more than a million programmers published in Science, and medical-diagnostics research as supporting deep interaction by talented, experienced humans. She describes the medical mechanism as complementary human and AI errors, and cites consulting and colonoscopy studies as warnings about shallow handoffs. These are reported cross-domain findings without detailed study citations or effect sizes in the transcript.
qs: the absolute best performance was when humans with real high levels of talent and experience interacted deeply with AI.
In that medical diagnostics paper, they called it complementary errors. AI and humans made different kinds of mistakes.
Filling out forms, pasting data back and forth. There's a lot of opportunities for automation, but then you fall into this trap of, well, we just need to string together automation after automation.

kp.k: Problem structure matters more than occupational skill labels
kp.d: Ming proposes distinguishing well-posed from ill-posed work rather than high-skill from low-skill jobs. She asserts that, given sufficient data, modern and agentic AI can outperform average workers and compete with top professionals on well-posed problems with known questions and solution procedures, including elite technical work. She locates humans' present relative advantage in uncertain problems where even the question is unclear. This is her general framework and capability assessment, not a legal-task benchmark.
qs: If there's enough data, it doesn't care if this is a job that an elite neurosurgeon used to do or a petroleum engineer.
Well-posed meaning we understand the problem, we know how to arrive at an answer.
We now live in a world where for most well-posed problems, modern AI, agentic AI, is simply better than the average person doing that job, competitive with the best professionals doing that job.
Forget the right answers, we don't even know what the question is. In that, humans have a relative advantage.

kp.k: New job creation may not absorb displaced workers
kp.d: Responding to the host's technological-job-creation argument, Ming uses textile mechanization and displaced craftspeople as a historical analogy for prolonged disruption despite eventual industry growth. She argues that demand for new jobs does not establish that humans will be qualified to supply the work, especially if AI can perform newly created well-posed tasks. She predicts more jobs but inadequate preparation for the roles in which humans retain an advantage; she provides no forecast horizon.
qs: we are being willfully naive of the massive disruption that happens in the interim.
Jevons is a statement about demand and not about supply.
as soon as it creates a new job, won't it be qualified to fill that job itself?
are we building a labor force that will be qualified to fill these new roles? And my prediction, born out of enormous amounts of data, is no, we won't.

kp.k: Intrinsic motivation predicts performance beyond financial incentives
kp.d: Ming describes 'endogenous motivation' as an internal willingness to invest effort rather than act principally for external rewards. From an analysis of 100,000 salespeople during her hiring-AI work in 2014, she reports that the best performers appeared least responsive to incentive timing, including selling immediately after a sales cycle ended. She says similar patterns appeared among software developers and in military career outcomes. She explicitly distinguishes earning bonuses from incentives causing superior performance.
qs: What I found in analyzing 100,000 salespeople, when I was the chief scientist of one of the first companies doing AI and hiring, believe it or not, way back in 2014
They got the most bonuses because they're the best salespeople. But that turns out to be a correlation rather than a cause.
the people who are most likely to make a sale the day after the end of the sales cycle, when the incentives are the least, are your best salespeople.

kp.k: Foundational human qualities predict careers and AI collaboration
kp.d: Ming describes work using a dataset of 122 million people to predict performance in jobs not yet held, including examining code, LinkedIn descriptions and Stack Overflow responses for 11 million working software developers. She reports that resilience, perspective taking, curiosity, growth mindset and cognitive capacities predicted career outcomes, and that foundational human qualities also predict successful AI use in her newer research. She emphasizes that many findings corroborated existing research rather than being discoveries unique to AI.
qs: I had a data set of 122 million people. And the job of my team was to figure out how good you are at jobs you've never held.

So we find things like resilience and perspective taking, your ability to understand the motivations of other people, curiosity, I noted it earlier, growth mindset, and some lower level cognitive things like numeracy and literacy and working memory span, how much stuff you can keep in mind.
They are predictive of positive life outcomes as well as career outcomes.
now in my new research, they are predictive of success in using AI.

kp.k: Curiosity and resilience can be deliberately developed
kp.d: Ming argues that these human qualities are measurable and, unlike some lower-level cognitive capacities in adulthood, changeable. She reports controlled resilience interventions associated with entrepreneurs remaining in business five years later more often than recipients of business or finance training. She also describes an experiment with eight-to-ten-year-olds in which training teachers to praise interesting questions rather than correct answers increased questioning, measured curiosity and engagement within six weeks. She recommends peer role modeling and organizational praise for inquiry, while reporting that productive public mistakes predicted faster graduation and better jobs in research with her wife.
qs: But there are standards for measuring these in psychology. I prefer to use behavior.
entrepreneurs getting a resilience intervention were much more likely to still be in business five years later
teachers were trained to praise interesting questions instead of right answers. And within just six weeks, these kids are asking more questions in class.
Being wrong in public, which is intellectual humility and curiosity, all rolled into one.

kp.k: Workload pressures encourage automation over capability development
kp.d: Using teachers' resistance to educational technology as her example, Ming argues that adoption reflects immediate workload constraints rather than simply unwillingness to improve outcomes. A tool promising reduced grading time addresses teachers' urgent needs more directly than one promising better long-term student outcomes. She generalizes that users often choose shallow interactions that make existing work easier instead of developing the capabilities required for a different kind of work.
qs: I've got a 60-hour-a-week job. I'm really only being paid for 40 of them. Sounds like you want me to have to learn an entirely new job.
They engage really shallowly in ways that make their lives easier rather than ways that essentially expand their capabilities.
So people select into automation instead of augmentation, and that's deeply problematic.

kp.k: Use AI as critical opposition, not an oracle
kp.d: Ming recommends deliberate deep engagement, challenging recommendations and retaining responsibility for thinking. Her 'nemesis prompt' asks AI to critique material she has written rather than write it for her, with the human also questioning the critique. She describes a script used first with her children and then herself to review a week's AI interactions for passive compliance, ignored good advice and constructive improvement. Its reported benefits are personal observations, not a controlled intervention result.
qs: What I would never allow it to do is write anything.
Read through it in detail and explain to me why I'm wrong and what I can do about it.
I am using it to make my work harder in the ways that make me better.
Here's where you simply did what the AI told you to do. Here's where it gave you good advice, but it looked like you ignored it. Here's where you took a good idea and you made it better.

kp.k: Benchmark joint capability rather than standalone model answers
kp.d: Ming reports that her experimental Socrates model, designed never to give answers, produced the highest rate of what she calls 'hybrid intelligence,' despite necessarily failing answer-based forecasting tests and standard benchmarks. She argues that standalone model performance does not measure whether AI improves human capabilities or well-being, asserts that no hybrid-intelligence benchmarks exist, and says her nonprofit is developing one. She also asserts that improving human capital currently offers greater AI productivity gains than improving models.
qs: There are more AI productivity gains to be made from higher human capital than from better models right now.
We built a model called Socrates that never gives answers.
Well, that highest rate of hybrid intelligence came from the Socrates model, the model which definitionally does the worst on standard benchmarks of AI.
Standard benchmarks measure how AI performs on their own. It doesn't tell you anything about whether this AI is making people better.
And so there literally are no hybrid intelligence benchmarks out there. So my nonprofit is working on one.

kp.k: Management should design integrated workflows around uncertainty
kp.d: Ming argues that traditional management's emphasis on reducing uncertainty can eliminate the work where humans retain relative advantage. She recommends either automating suitable activities or deeply integrating human and machine work, rather than maintaining parallel streams with sequential handoffs. She reports seeing few organizations adopt this approach, while highly talented workers are already doing so independently; these are her observations and recommendations, not quantified organizational findings.
qs: humanity's unique relative advantage here is our ability to deal with uncertainty and explore the unknown. If you manage that away, then you probably might as well just deploy a bunch of robots.
Don't build parallel workstreams where AI automates something up to a point, and then maybe a human takes on over that.
Something is either automatable or it should be cyborged.
I am not really seeing many organizations where that's coming through, but what we are seeing is elite level, highly talented workers are doing this on their own right now.

kp.k: Automating junior legal work threatens professional formation
kp.d: Ming explicitly asks how junior lawyers will become partners if case preparation, contract review and other intensive entry-level work no longer require them. She draws analogous concerns from medical residency, junior coding and graduate scientific analysis, framing the development of future experts as a collective-action problem. She calls for a different conception of entry-level elite work but does not specify a replacement training model or present legal-sector employment data.
qs: How are your junior employees ever going to become those new elite workers?

How do you become an elite, how do you become a partner at a law firm if no one needs you to do case prep and contract review and all the 80-hour-a-week stuff, that's the horror stories of being a junior lawyer
We need a very different way to think about entry-level work in elite world

kp.k: Policy should address potential workforce polarization
kp.d: Ming's closing conditional forecast is not a universal jobs collapse but a divided labor market: strong demand for scarce elite workers alongside undesirable jobs for people unable to enter that group. She calls for global policy attention to workers not ready for elite work and for helping more people cross that divide. The forecast is prospective and unquantified, rather than an observed legal-market outcome.
qs: What happens in our current workforce if my prediction comes true, and there's lots of new jobs, and it's all for an elite labor force that we simply don't have enough population to fill
It's not a jobs apocalypse. There'll be lots of terrible jobs too.
We need to figure out how to pull more people across that divide.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Vivienne Ming claims that deeply integrated human–AI collaboration can outperform AI alone, whereas copying AI answers or delegating analysis before human approval does not provide the same benefit.
pts.d: In her forecasting experiment, Ming distinguishes 'cyborgs', who challenged the AI, examined underlying data and co-created predictions throughout, from people who copied answers and from 'Centaur' users who delegated analysis and then made a decision. She reports that cyborgs outperformed AI and nearly matched the prediction market, while the latter decision-making arrangement performed worse than AI alone. This is a cross-domain forecasting finding, not a demonstrated result for legal work. Her account also states that even the weakest AI tested outperformed the best unaided participant, whose relevant subject knowledge was limited.

pts.k: Ming argues that AI's capability boundary follows well-posed versus ill-posed problems rather than conventional high-skill versus low-skill occupations.
pts.d: She claims that, with sufficient data, modern AI can perform well-defined components of prestigious technical jobs at the level of leading professionals and outperform the average worker. Human comparative advantage remains in uncertainty, problem formulation and situations where the relevant question is not yet known. She endorses automation of activities such as form filling and data transfer, but recommends deeply integrated collaboration for work that is not fully automatable.

pts.k: Ming predicts that creating additional jobs will not automatically protect displaced workers because AI may itself be qualified to perform the new jobs.
pts.d: She expects more jobs rather than a universal disappearance of employment, but predicts an inadequate supply of people prepared for new elite work. She warns of a division between workers capable of tackling uncertain, complex problems with AI and people left with undesirable work. Her historical discussion of weaving and industrialisation supplies an analogy for disruptive transitions, rather than direct evidence of future AI employment outcomes.

pts.k: Ming warns that automating junior legal tasks threatens the traditional pathway by which junior lawyers develop into partners.
pts.d: Her specific legal-profession claim concerns the developmental function of case preparation and contract review. If firms no longer need juniors to perform those activities, they must find another way to develop future experts. She presents comparable problems for medical residents, junior programmers and graduate researchers. This is a conditional warning about training and progression, not a quantified forecast of associate redundancies or changes in law-firm staffing ratios.

pts.k: Ming claims that foundational human capabilities predict effective AI use and offer a larger immediate productivity opportunity than further model improvement.
pts.d: She identifies curiosity, intellectual humility, perspective taking, resilience, growth mindset and endogenous motivation as relevant capabilities. She says many are measurable, predictive of positive outcomes and changeable, unlike some lower-level cognitive characteristics that she regards as largely established by adulthood. She recommends role modelling and rewarding questions rather than only correct answers. The claim that human-capital improvement offers greater AI productivity gains is broad and unquantified in the interview.

pts.k: Ming claims that everyday incentives encourage shallow automation rather than capability-enhancing augmentation, and that management practices need to change.
pts.d: She argues that time-pressured workers tend to choose tools that reduce their immediate workload rather than tools that expand their abilities. At the organisational level, she says the established managerial aim of reducing uncertainty can suppress the area where humans retain comparative advantage. She reports that highly talented workers are already developing integrated AI practices individually, while she sees few organisations building such workflows systematically. Her recommendations include using AI as a critical opponent rather than an oracle, with the human continuing to examine and challenge its advice.

pts.k: Ming claims that standalone AI benchmarks miss whether a model improves human performance, and that an answer-withholding model produced the strongest collaborative outcome in her experiment.
pts.d: She describes her Socrates model as refusing to supply answers, thereby failing conventional answer-based tests while producing the highest rate of what she calls 'hybrid intelligence'. She argues for measuring the emergent performance of humans and AI together rather than treating model-only scores as evidence of augmentation. She says her nonprofit is developing a benchmark for this purpose. These statements concern benchmarking, not human verification of legal outputs or any named legal-AI benchmark.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Ming draws on her own forecasting and workforce research, references to other studies, historical analogies and personal experience; the interview does not supply a legal-services experiment or detailed study documentation.
pts.d: For forecasting, she describes recruitment around UC Berkeley and Greater Berkeley, ten predictions in one hour, future-event questions chosen to avoid memorised answers, and comparisons with standalone models and Polymarket. She estimates cyborg behaviour at about 10% among Berkeley students and 5% in the wider population she examined, then speculates that prevalence may be in the low single digits in the general population. No total sample size, model list, accuracy table or statistical uncertainty is supplied. For broader collaboration claims, she invokes Anthropic research, a Science analysis involving more than a million programmers, medical diagnostics research on complementary errors, and studies involving BCG consultants and colonoscopies, without full citations or effect sizes. For human capabilities, she cites a 122-million-person workforce dataset, analysis of 100,000 salespeople, software-developer research, and educational and resilience interventions. Her personal use of AI to critique writing and a weekly AI-interaction report used with her children are experiential examples. The junior-lawyer warning and labour-market predictions are extrapolations rather than reported legal-sector findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Ming presents capability and adoption claims as current at the time of this 2026 interview; workforce polarisation and training disruption are conditional predictions without a deadline.
pts.d: Her current-performance claims depend on sufficient data and well-posed tasks. Superior collaboration depends on active, sustained human engagement with the data and reasoning, and she emphasises talent and experience in the other studies she discusses. She does not claim that merely retaining a human approval step improves outcomes. The forecasting participants were initially non-experts in the selected questions. Her employment warning depends on new work requiring capabilities the workforce has not developed, and her legal-training warning depends on junior tasks becoming unnecessary. She provides no timetable for the elimination of particular legal tasks, changes to partnership progression or economy-wide polarisation. Developing human capabilities and redesigning management are presented as opportunities to alter these outcomes.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly identified legal stakeholders are junior lawyers and law firms responsible for developing future partners; the wider claims concern workers, managers, educators and AI developers.
pts.d: Junior lawyers face a potential loss of learning-through-work opportunities, and law firms face a future-expertise development problem. Experienced, highly capable professionals may gain from integrated AI use. Workers who primarily reproduce AI answers or lack the capabilities demanded by new roles face displacement or reduced access to desirable work. Managers must reconsider workflow and development practices; educators and parents are asked to cultivate curiosity and resilience; AI developers are asked to design and benchmark augmentation rather than only automation. Ming's legal example does not distinguish firm size, practice area or jurisdiction, and the interview does not establish specific effects on legal fees, client outcomes or access to justice.
